Autoencoders and CNN-Based Autoencoders for Modal Decomposition¶

This notebook trains deep neural networks to perform non-linear dimensionality reduction on flow-field data:

v(x, y) -> Encoder -> z (latent space, d << nx*ny*nv) -> Decoder -> v_hat(x, y)

It is the companion of a U-Net notebook on turbulent-field time stepping (a separate project). While that notebook trained a network to advance a field forward in time, this notebook trains networks to compress a field into a low-dimensional latent space and reconstruct it (an autoencoder), and to approximate the temporal evolution inside that latent space (a Koopman-operator autoencoder).

Three architectures are covered, in increasing order of complexity:

1. Dense (fully connected) autoencoder            -- non-linear PCA/POD
2. Dense autoencoder + linear Koopman operator     -- non-linear PCA/POD + linear dynamics
3. Convolutional autoencoder                       -- exploits spatial locality

The dataset is a 2D DNS simulation of viscous flow past two collinear plates (Reynolds number 100), stored as a 4D array of shape (n_t, n_x, n_y, n_v), where n_v = 2 corresponds to the velocity components u and v.

Stage 1 — Compressing a flow field: dense and convolutional autoencoders against POD¶

Portfolio project: compress, structure and evolve one flow dataset — autoencoders, a VAE and a Koopman autoencoder.

The dataset is a 2-D simulation of viscous flow past two collinear plates at Reynolds number 100: 1,000 snapshots of the velocity (u, v) on a 128 × 64 grid, a state of 16,384 numbers per snapshot. This notebook compresses each snapshot (mean flow removed) into 10 numbers and back, with a dense autoencoder (flatten, 512 hidden units, 10 latent numbers; 16.8 million weights) and a convolutional one (one 3 × 3 convolution with 32 filters and one pooling level; 1.4 million weights), and compares both with POD truncated at 10 modes, the best linear compression of the same size. It shows what the latent "modes" of an autoencoder are and are not, and which architecture suits which job. I solve its three experiments (latent size, a deeper convolutional autoencoder, latent trajectories against POD coefficients), repeat every training with the seeds 0, 1 and 2, and record a training animation.

How it connects. Stages 2 and 3 reload the same dataset and re-implement this notebook's dense builders, split, error measure and POD; Stage 4 compares POD, autoencoders and a VAE across latent sizes and runs the rollouts.

About the outputs. The outputs below come from my single run (Apple M3 Max, 2026-10-13), on the CPU only: the convolutional networks train about 17 times slower per step on the Apple GPU, and mixing devices in one process slowed them further, so the whole notebook runs on the CPU (dense 6 minutes, convolutional 10 minutes). Afterwards I changed only text for this repository: this cell and the paths cell, the path lines (dataset from ../release_assets/, models to ../models/01_autoencoders_and_pod/, tables to ../results/01_autoencoders_and_pod/, animation to ../animations/01_*), comments, labels and printed text. The POD error is computed on all snapshots while the autoencoders are scored on the validation snapshots; Stage 4 adds POD fitted on the training snapshots only.

4. Load the Dataset and Basic Statistics¶

The dataset is a NumPy compressed archive (.npz), storing the velocity field UV together with the spatial grid coordinates x and y. .npz files are convenient because they store several arrays in one file, load fast, and preserve array names.

We also remove the mean flow: for a better visualization and to avoid large differences in scale across the domain, the time-averaged field is subtracted from every snapshot.

In [5]:
# =========================================================
# Load the NumPy compressed archive
# =========================================================

data = np.load(data_file)

print("Available keys:", data.files)

# Velocity field, shape (n_t, n_x, n_y, n_v)
v = data["UV"]

# Spatial coordinate arrays
xx = data["x"]
yy = data["y"]

print("Velocity field shape:", v.shape)
print("UV statistics:")
print("  min: ", np.min(v))
print("  max: ", np.max(v))
print("  mean:", np.mean(v))
print("  std: ", np.std(v))

6. Train/Validation Split¶

The dataset is split 80/20 into training and validation snapshots. Unlike the U-Net time-stepping project, here the network never needs pairs of consecutive snapshots for the plain autoencoder task: every snapshot is both input and target (reconstruction).

In [8]:

# =========================================================

n_t, n_x, n_y, n_v = v.shape

v_trn, v_val = train_test_split(
    v,
    test_size=0.2,
    random_state=24,
    shuffle=True
)

print("Total snapshots:  ", n_t)
print("Training snapshots:  ", v_trn.shape[0])
print("Validation snapshots:", v_val.shape[0])

# Dimensionality of the latent (encoded) space

n_state_variables = n_x * n_y * n_v
print("Full state dimension:", n_state_variables)

7. Dense Autoencoder: Encoder and Decoder Building Blocks¶

An autoencoder is built from two parts:

encoder (phi):  v (n_x, n_y, n_v) -> z in R^d          (non-linear dimensionality reduction)
decoder (psi):  z in R^d          -> v_hat (n_x, n_y, n_v)

The encoder flattens the spatial field into a single state vector, passes it through a dense hidden layer that learns non-linear combinations of the original degrees of freedom, and projects it onto the low-dimensional latent space. The decoder performs the inverse mapping. Together they define a non-linear analogue of Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD): the network learns to compress the field into d degrees of freedom while minimizing the reconstruction error.

In [9]:
# =========================================================
# Dense encoder / decoder building blocks
# =========================================================


def create_dense_encoder(
    input_shape,
    latent_dim,
    hidden_units=512, # What happens if you change this to 256 or 1024?
    activation="relu"
):
    """
    Create a dense (fully connected) encoder.

    Flattens the spatial field into a state vector, passes it through one
    hidden layer, and projects it onto a d-dimensional latent space.
    """

    inputs = tf.keras.layers.Input(shape=input_shape)

    x = tf.keras.layers.Flatten()(inputs)
    x = tf.keras.layers.Dense(hidden_units, activation=activation)(x)

    latent = tf.keras.layers.Dense(latent_dim)(x)

    encoder = tf.keras.Model(inputs, latent, name="dense_encoder")

    return encoder


def create_dense_decoder(
    output_shape,
    latent_dim,
    hidden_units=512, # What happens if you change this to 256 or 1024?
    activation="relu",
    dropout_rate=0.2
):
    """
    Create a dense (fully connected) decoder.

    Mirrors create_dense_encoder(): expands the latent vector through one
    hidden layer, then reconstructs the flattened state and reshapes it back
    to the original spatial dimensions.
    """

    n_x, n_y, n_v = output_shape
    n_state_variables = n_x * n_y * n_v

    latent_inputs = tf.keras.layers.Input(shape=(latent_dim,))

    x = tf.keras.layers.Dense(hidden_units, activation=activation)(latent_inputs)
    x = tf.keras.layers.Dense(n_state_variables)(x)

    # Droput is better in the decoder after the hidden layer, not after the output layer.
    # x = tf.keras.layers.Dropout(dropout_rate)(x)

    outputs = tf.keras.layers.Reshape(output_shape)(x)

    decoder = tf.keras.Model(latent_inputs, outputs, name="dense_decoder")

    return decoder

8. Assemble, Train and Save the Dense Autoencoder¶

The full autoencoder chains encoder and decoder together:

v -> encoder -> z -> decoder -> v_hat

and is trained to minimize the mean-squared reconstruction error, with inputs and targets both equal to v_trn. As in the U-Net projects, we use EarlyStopping (monitoring the validation loss) and ReduceLROnPlateau to make training robust without having to hand-tune the number of epochs.

In [10]:
# =========================================================
# Assemble the dense autoencoder
# =========================================================

input_shape = (n_x, n_y, n_v)

dense_encoder = create_dense_encoder(input_shape, latent_dim=latent_dim)
dense_decoder = create_dense_decoder(input_shape, latent_dim=latent_dim)

dense_encoder.summary()
dense_decoder.summary()

inputs = tf.keras.layers.Input(shape=input_shape)
outputs = dense_decoder(dense_encoder(inputs))

dense_autoencoder = tf.keras.Model(
    inputs,
    outputs,
    name="Dense_Autoencoder"
)

dense_autoencoder.compile(
    optimizer=tf.keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=1e-3),
    loss="mse"
)

dense_autoencoder.summary()

Hook before the training cells. Checkpoints for the notebook's dense and convolutional autoencoder trainings (best model by validation loss, periodic checkpoint every 60 epochs, in ../models/01_autoencoders_and_pod/checkpoints/), and, for the dense autoencoder, a snapshot collector for the training animation, so the animation comes from the base run (no second training). The training cells add these callbacks to the notebook's early stopping and learning-rate schedule; nothing else changes.

In [11]:
import os
from pathlib import Path
EX_CKPT = Path("../models/01_autoencoders_and_pod/checkpoints"); EX_CKPT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
class ExPeriodicCheckpoint(tf.keras.callbacks.Callback):
    def __init__(self, path, every): super().__init__(); self.path, self.every = path, max(1, int(every))
    def on_epoch_end(self, epoch, logs=None):
        if (epoch + 1) % self.every == 0: self.model.save_weights(str(self.path))
def ex_ckpt_callbacks(name, epochs, monitor="val_loss"):
    return [tf.keras.callbacks.ModelCheckpoint(str(EX_CKPT / f"{name}_best.weights.h5"), monitor=monitor, save_best_only=True, save_weights_only=True),
            ExPeriodicCheckpoint(EX_CKPT / f"{name}_periodic.weights.h5", epochs // 10)]
class ExAnimSnapshots(tf.keras.callbacks.Callback):
    def __init__(self, x_one, x_val): super().__init__(); self.x1, self.xv = x_one, x_val; self.snaps = []; self.loss = []; self.val = []
    def _snap(self, e):
        pv = self.model.predict(self.xv, verbose=0)
        err = float(np.mean(np.linalg.norm(self.xv - pv, axis=(1, 2)) / np.linalg.norm(self.xv, axis=(1, 2))))
        self.snaps.append(dict(epoch=e, rec=self.model(self.x1, training=False).numpy()[0], loss=list(self.loss), val=list(self.val), err=err))
    def on_train_begin(self, logs=None): self._snap(0)
    def on_epoch_end(self, epoch, logs=None): self.loss.append(logs["loss"]); self.val.append(logs["val_loss"]); self._snap(epoch + 1)
ANIM_CB = None
EX_TIMES = {}   # wall time of each base training, to decide which trainings get seed repeats (15-minute rule)
class ExTimer(tf.keras.callbacks.Callback):
    def __init__(self, name): super().__init__(); self.name = name
    def on_train_begin(self, logs=None): import time; self.t0 = time.time()
    def on_train_end(self, logs=None): import time; EX_TIMES[self.name] = time.time() - self.t0
def ex_base_callbacks(name):
    global ANIM_CB
    cbs = ex_ckpt_callbacks(name, 600) + [ExTimer(name)]
    if name == "dense_ae":
        ANIM_CB = ExAnimSnapshots(v_val[-1:], v_val); cbs.append(ANIM_CB)
    return cbs

# =========================================================
# Train the dense autoencoder
# =========================================================

early_stopping = tf.keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(
    monitor="val_loss",
    patience=20,
    restore_best_weights=True
)

reduce_lr = tf.keras.callbacks.ReduceLROnPlateau(
    monitor="val_loss",
    factor=0.5,
    patience=8,
    min_lr=1e-6
)

history_dense = dense_autoencoder.fit(
    v_trn,
    v_trn,
    validation_data=(v_val, v_val),
    epochs=600,
    batch_size=32,
    # [original] callbacks=[early_stopping, reduce_lr],
    callbacks=[early_stopping, reduce_lr] + ex_base_callbacks("dense_ae"),  # added: checkpoints and animation snapshots
    verbose=2
)

Overfitting in the Dense Autoencoder¶

The training curve shows a typical overfitting pattern:

  • The training loss keeps decreasing steadily throughout training.
  • The validation loss stops improving much earlier (around epoch 40-50) and plateaus at a clearly higher value.
  • The gap between the two curves keeps widening.

This happens because the model has enough capacity to memorize specific details of the training snapshots that don't represent general flow patterns, instead of learning a latent representation that generalizes to new data (the validation set).

Why the error plateaus instead of blowing up: EarlyStopping with restore_best_weights=True stops training and restores the weights from the best validation point, so we never see the model degrade beyond that point.

Likely causes and mitigations, from most to least probable:

  1. Lack of variance normalization — only the mean is subtracted, not divided by the standard deviation. This makes optimization harder and complicates interpreting the magnitude of the error.
  2. Too much capacity for the dataset size — hidden_units=512 may be excessive relative to the number of available snapshots. Reduce the hidden layer size or add Dropout.
  3. Lack of explicit regularization — L2 kernel_regularizer could be added to the dense layers.
  4. Limited training data — if this is the real bottleneck, increasing the dataset (more snapshots or data augmentation) helps more than any architectural change.

How to properly evaluate it: compare the relative reconstruction error (Section 10 of the notebook) against the POD baseline at the same latent_dim (Section 11), rather than judging the raw MSE in isolation.

10. Evaluate Reconstruction Quality¶

We compute the mean relative $\ell_2$-norm reconstruction error over all snapshots,

$$ \epsilon = \frac{1}{n_t}\sum_{i=1}^{n_t}\frac{\lVert v_i - \hat v_i \rVert}{\lVert v_i \rVert}, $$

and visualize one validation snapshot against its reconstruction.

In [16]:
# =========================================================
# Relative reconstruction error
# =========================================================

def relative_reconstruction_error(v_true, v_pred):
    """
    Mean relative L2-norm reconstruction error over all snapshots and
    variables.

    Parameters
    ----------
    v_true, v_pred: arrays of shape (n_t, n_x, n_y, n_v)

    Returns
    -------
    err: float, mean relative error
    """

    err = np.linalg.norm(v_true - v_pred, axis=(1, 2)) / np.linalg.norm(
        v_true, axis=(1, 2)
    )
    err = np.mean(err, axis=0)

    return err


v_val_rec = dense_autoencoder.predict(v_val)

dense_ae_error = relative_reconstruction_error(v_val, v_val_rec)
print("Dense autoencoder mean relative reconstruction error:", dense_ae_error)

11. Baseline: Reconstruction via POD¶

Before trusting the autoencoder, we compare it against the optimal linear low-rank approximation given by Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD). The data is reshaped into a snapshot matrix $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{(n_x n_y n_v) \times n_t}$, a truncated SVD is computed, and the field is reconstructed using only the first d modes. Since POD is the optimal linear low-rank approximation, this comparison highlights the potential advantage of the autoencoder's non-linear compression.

In [18]:
# =========================================================
# POD baseline via truncated SVD
# =========================================================

U, s, vh = np.linalg.svd(
    v.reshape((n_t, -1)).T,
    full_matrices=False
)

v_pod = U[:, :latent_dim] @ np.diag(s[:latent_dim]) @ vh[:latent_dim]
v_pod = v_pod.T.reshape((-1, n_x, n_y, n_v))

pod_error = relative_reconstruction_error(v, v_pod)

print(f"POD baseline mean relative reconstruction error ({latent_dim} modes):", pod_error)
print("Dense autoencoder mean relative reconstruction error:               ", dense_ae_error)

if dense_ae_error.mean() < pod_error.mean():
    print("\nThe autoencoder improves on the linear POD baseline.")
else:
    print("\nThe autoencoder does not improve on the linear POD baseline yet.")

# =========================================================
# "Modes" of the plain (non-variational) autoencoder
# =========================================================

z_all = dense_encoder.predict(v, verbose=0)
z_center = z_all.mean(axis=0)
z_std = z_all.std(axis=0)

baseline = dense_decoder.predict(z_center[None, :], verbose=0)[0]

mode_fields = []
mode_norms = []

for i in range(latent_dim):
    z_perturbed = z_center.copy()
    z_perturbed[i] += 2 * z_std[i]
    field = dense_decoder.predict(z_perturbed[None, :], verbose=0)[0] - baseline
    mode_fields.append(field)
    mode_norms.append(np.linalg.norm(field))

order = np.argsort(mode_norms)[::-1]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 5, figsize=(20, 8))
plt.set_cmap("RdBu_r")

for rank, (ax, idx) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, order)):
    ax.contourf(xx, yy, mode_fields[idx][:, :, 0], levels=20)
    ax.set_title(f"AE latent dim {idx+1}  (rank {rank+1}, |effect|={mode_norms[idx]:.2f})")
    ax.set_aspect("equal")

fig.suptitle("Decoded effect of each dense-autoencoder latent dimension (u-component)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Can every field be recovered by summing these modes?¶

With POD, yes. Any field in the dataset (up to the truncation error from using only d modes) is recovered exactly as the mean field plus a sum of spatial modes weighted by their temporal coefficients -- that additive reconstruction is literally the definition of the decomposition.

With the AE/VAE, no. What we plotted as "modes" for the autoencoder is only a sensitivity diagnostic: how the decoded field changes when one latent dimension is perturbed from the center, holding the others fixed. This is not a basis you can linearly combine to reconstruct an arbitrary field, because the decoder is a non-linear function:

$$ \text{decoder}(z_1) + \text{decoder}(z_2) + \dots \;\neq\; \text{decoder}(z_1 + z_2 + \dots) $$

To recover a specific field from the AE/VAE, you need that field's actual latent vector -- obtained by passing it through the encoder -- and decoded all dimensions at once, in a single forward pass:

z_real = dense_encoder.predict(v[t_idx:t_idx+1], verbose=0)
v_reconstructed = dense_decoder.predict(z_real, verbose=0)[0]

Summing the individual per-dimension "mode" fields instead will not reproduce this result.

Summary: for POD, the modes are the building blocks -- summation is how reconstruction works. For the AE/VAE, the full latent vector (all dimensions together, passed through the non-linear decoder) encodes the field; the individual "modes" are useful only for inspecting what each latent direction does on its own, not for reconstructing anything by addition.

A note on energy¶

The MSE loss minimized by the autoencoder is, for a velocity field, proportional to the kinetic energy of the reconstruction error:

$$ \text{MSE} \;\propto\; \int |v - \hat v|^2\, dx \;\sim\; \text{residual energy} $$

This is the same quantity POD minimizes, which is why comparing dense_ae_error against pod_error at the same d is a fair comparison -- both live in the same energy metric.

What differs is how that energy is distributed across dimensions. POD splits it additively and in order: mode 1 captures sigma_1^2, mode 2 adds sigma_2^2 more, and so on -- a direct consequence of the SVD (Eckart-Young). The autoencoder has no such split: it minimizes the joint error energy across all d latent dimensions at once, through a non-linear model, with no guarantee that any one dimension carries a well-defined, additive "share" of energy the way a POD mode does.

In short: the training objective is an energy measure, but the per-dimension energy breakdown that POD gives for free does not exist for the AE/VAE.

Recovering spatial information¶

Dense vs. Convolutional Autoencoders: When to Use Which¶

A quick reference for choosing between a dense (flatten-based) and a convolutional autoencoder architecture, across the U-Net and latent-space notebooks.

Criterion Dense (Flatten) Convolutional
Spatial structure of the data Ignored — the field is flattened into a vector, losing all notion of which pixel is next to which Exploited directly — filters act on local neighborhoods
Number of parameters Grows with n_x * n_y * n_v * hidden_units — explodes with resolution Filters are shared across the whole domain — parameter count does not depend on spatial resolution
Amount of data needed Needs more training snapshots to avoid overfitting Generalizes better with less data, thanks to parameter sharing and the locality inductive bias
Translation invariance None — a structure shifted by a few pixels looks like a different input to the network Approximately invariant — a filter recognizes the same pattern wherever it appears
Computational cost (training) Cheaper per layer, but offset by the larger number of parameters More efficient per parameter, though each convolution is more expensive per individual operation
Type of structure captured best Global correlations between distant points in the domain (any-point-to-any-point relationships) Local, multi-scale patterns (coherent structures, streaks, vortices), built up hierarchically through pooling levels
Latent space interpretability Each latent dimension can mix information from the whole domain, with no direct spatial meaning Easier to relate to specific physical regions/structures, especially if activation maps are kept
When both perform similarly Small or spatially unstructured domains, where there is little local pattern to exploit —
Examples in these projects Dense AE (this notebook, Sections 7-8); Koopman autoencoder (Stage 3, needs flattening for the linear operator) Convolutional AE (this notebook, Sections 12-16); U-Nets (separate projects)

Rule of thumb¶

If the field has real 2D/3D spatial structure (as in essentially all of our turbulence work), convolutions are almost always the better choice. Dense architectures are mainly justified when you need the latent space to be explicitly compatible with something linear downstream — which is exactly why the Koopman autoencoder in Stage 3 still uses a dense encoder/decoder: not out of convenience, but because that specific structure requires it.

12. Understanding Convolutional Building Blocks¶

Before building a convolutional autoencoder, we briefly inspect what convolution, pooling and upsampling each do to a spatial field, as building intuition for these operators.

A 2D convolutional layer applies a set of learnable $H \times H \times K$ filters:

$$ x^{(l)}_{ijm} = \varphi\!\left( \sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{p=1}^{H}\sum_{q=1}^{H} x^{(l-1)}_{i+p,\,j+q,\,k}\, w^{(l)}_{pqkm} + b^{(l)}_{ijm} \right), $$

where $x^{(l-1)}$, $x^{(l)}$ are the input/output feature maps, $w^{(l)}$, $b^{(l)}$ are learnable weights/biases, and $\varphi(\cdot)$ is a non-linear activation.

In [21]:
# =========================================================
# Effect of a single 2D convolution on a spatial field
# =========================================================

xin = v[-1:, :, :, 0:1].astype(dtype=np.float32)
print("xin shape:", xin.shape)

yc = tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(
    filters=1,
    kernel_size=(3, 3),
    strides=(1, 1),
    padding="same"
)(xin)
yc = yc.numpy()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(16, 4))
ax[0].imshow(xin.squeeze().T, cmap="binary")
ax[0].set_title("Input field")
ax[1].imshow(yc.squeeze().T, cmap="binary")
ax[1].set_title("After 3x3 convolution")
plt.show()

xin shape: (1, 128, 64, 1)

# Spatial downsampling using max pooling
# =========================================================

max_pool_2d = tf.keras.layers.MaxPooling2D(pool_size=2, padding="same")
ymp = max_pool_2d(xin).numpy()

print("Pooled field shape:", ymp.shape)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(16, 4))
ax[0].imshow(xin.squeeze().T, cmap="binary")
ax[0].set_title("Input field")
ax[1].imshow(ymp.squeeze().T, cmap="binary")

# =========================================================
# Spatial upsampling of feature maps
# =========================================================

upsample_2d = tf.keras.layers.UpSampling2D(size=2)
yup = upsample_2d(ymp).numpy()

print("Upsampled field shape:", yup.shape)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4))
ax[0].imshow(xin.squeeze().T, cmap="binary")
ax[0].set_title("Input field")
ax[1].imshow(ymp.squeeze().T, cmap="binary")
ax[1].set_title("After max pooling")
ax[2].imshow(yup.squeeze().T, cmap="binary")
ax[2].set_title("After upsampling")
plt.show()

Upsampled field shape: (1, 128, 64, 1)

Convolution learns local spatial filters, max pooling compresses the field by retaining the strongest local responses (reducing computational cost and adding a degree of spatial invariance), and upsampling restores the grid resolution without adding new information. Combining all three is the basis of the convolutional autoencoder built next.

13. Convolutional Autoencoder: Encoder and Decoder Architecture¶

This architecture exploits the spatial structure of the data directly (unlike the dense autoencoder, which discards it after Flatten()). One convolutional layer extracts local spatial features, one max-pooling layer halves the spatial resolution, and a dense layer maps the resulting feature maps onto the latent space. The decoder mirrors this: a dense layer expands the latent vector, a convolution refines the feature maps, and an upsampling layer restores the original resolution.

In [24]:
# =========================================================
# Convolutional encoder / decoder building blocks
# =========================================================


def create_conv_encoder(
    input_shape,
    latent_dim,
    n_filters=32,
    kernel_size=3,
    pool_size=2,
    activation="relu"
):
    """
    Create a convolutional encoder.

    One Conv2D layer extracts local spatial features (resolution unchanged,
    padding="same"), one MaxPooling2D layer halves the spatial resolution,
    and a Dense layer projects the flattened feature maps onto the
    d-dimensional latent space.
    """

    inputs = tf.keras.layers.Input(shape=input_shape)

    x = tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(
        filters=n_filters,
        kernel_size=kernel_size,
        activation=activation,
        padding="same"
    )(inputs)

    x = tf.keras.layers.MaxPooling2D(pool_size=pool_size, padding="same")(x)

    x = tf.keras.layers.Flatten()(x)
    latent = tf.keras.layers.Dense(latent_dim)(x)

    encoder = tf.keras.Model(inputs, latent, name="conv_encoder")

    return encoder


def create_conv_decoder(
    output_shape,
    latent_dim,
    n_filters=32,
    kernel_size=3,
    pool_size=2,
    activation="relu"
):
    """
    Create a convolutional decoder, mirroring create_conv_encoder().

    A Dense layer expands the latent vector into a tensor compatible with
    the pooled feature-map size, a Conv2D layer refines the spatial
    features, an UpSampling2D layer restores the original resolution, and a
    final Conv2D layer (linear activation) maps back to n_v channels.
    """

    n_x, n_y, n_v = output_shape

    # Spatial size after the encoder's pooling operation
    h_enc = int(np.ceil(n_x / pool_size))
    w_enc = int(np.ceil(n_y / pool_size))

    latent_inputs = tf.keras.layers.Input(shape=(latent_dim,))

    x = tf.keras.layers.Dense(
        h_enc * w_enc * n_filters,
        activation=activation
    )(latent_inputs)

    x = tf.keras.layers.Reshape((h_enc, w_enc, n_filters))(x)

    x = tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(
        filters=n_filters,
        kernel_size=kernel_size,
        activation=activation,
        padding="same"
    )(x)

    x = tf.keras.layers.UpSampling2D(size=pool_size)(x)

    # Crop back to the exact original size, in case pooling rounded up
    x = tf.keras.layers.Cropping2D(
        cropping=((0, x.shape[1] - n_x), (0, x.shape[2] - n_y))
    )(x)

    outputs = tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(
        filters=n_v,
        kernel_size=kernel_size,
        activation=None,
        padding="same"
    )(x)

    decoder = tf.keras.Model(latent_inputs, outputs, name="conv_decoder")

    return decoder

14. Assemble, Train and Save the Convolutional Autoencoder¶

Same training recipe as the dense autoencoder (EarlyStopping + ReduceLROnPlateau), applied to the convolutional architecture.

In [25]:
# modified: the convolutional autoencoder is built on the CPU (UpSampling2D trains about 17 times slower on the Apple GPU)
with tf.device("/CPU:0"):
    # =========================================================
    # Assemble the convolutional autoencoder
    # =========================================================

    conv_encoder = create_conv_encoder(input_shape, latent_dim=latent_dim)
    conv_decoder = create_conv_decoder(input_shape, latent_dim=latent_dim)

    conv_encoder.summary()
    conv_decoder.summary()

    conv_inputs = tf.keras.layers.Input(shape=input_shape)
    conv_outputs = conv_decoder(conv_encoder(conv_inputs))

    conv_autoencoder = tf.keras.Model(
        conv_inputs,
        conv_outputs,
        name="Conv_Autoencoder"
    )

    conv_autoencoder.compile(
        optimizer=tf.keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=1e-3),
        loss="mse"
    )

    conv_autoencoder.summary()

# modified: the convolutional autoencoder trains on the CPU (step timing in the device cell)
with tf.device("/CPU:0"):
    # =========================================================
    # Train the convolutional autoencoder
    # =========================================================

    early_stopping = tf.keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(
        monitor="val_loss",
        patience=20,
        restore_best_weights=True
    )

    reduce_lr = tf.keras.callbacks.ReduceLROnPlateau(
        monitor="val_loss",
        factor=0.5,
        patience=8,
        min_lr=1e-6
    )

    history_conv = conv_autoencoder.fit(
        v_trn,
        v_trn,
        validation_data=(v_val, v_val),
        epochs=600,
        batch_size=32,
        # [original] callbacks=[early_stopping, reduce_lr],
        callbacks=[early_stopping, reduce_lr] + ex_base_callbacks("conv_ae"),  # added: checkpoints
        verbose=2
    )

15. Evaluate the Convolutional Autoencoder¶

We compare the convolutional autoencoder against the dense autoencoder and the POD baseline, all using the same latent dimension d, and visualize one reconstructed validation snapshot.

In [28]:
# =========================================================
# Evaluate and compare all three approaches
# =========================================================

v_val_rec_conv = conv_autoencoder.predict(v_val)

conv_ae_error = relative_reconstruction_error(v_val, v_val_rec_conv)

print(f"Reconstruction error comparison (latent dimension d = {latent_dim}):")
print("  POD baseline (linear):        ", pod_error)
print("  Dense autoencoder (non-linear):", dense_ae_error)
print("  Conv autoencoder (non-linear): ", conv_ae_error)

vmin0, vmax0 = v_val[idx, :, :, 0].min(), v_val[idx, :, :, 0].max()
vmin1, vmax1 = v_val[idx, :, :, 1].min(), v_val[idx, :, :, 1].max()

ax[0, 0].contourf(xx, yy, v_val[idx, :, :, 0], levels=20, vmin=vmin0, vmax=vmax0)
ax[1, 0].contourf(xx, yy, v_val[idx, :, :, 1], levels=20, vmin=vmin1, vmax=vmax1)

ax[0, 1].contourf(xx, yy, v_val_rec_conv[idx, :, :, 0], levels=20, vmin=vmin0, vmax=vmax0)
ax[1, 1].contourf(xx, yy, v_val_rec_conv[idx, :, :, 1], levels=20, vmin=vmin1, vmax=vmax1)

ax[0, 0].set_ylabel("y")
ax[1, 0].set_ylabel("y")
ax[1, 0].set_xlabel("x")
ax[1, 1].set_xlabel("x")

ax[0, 0].set_title(r"$u$ reference")
ax[1, 0].set_title(r"$v$ reference")
ax[0, 1].set_title(r"$u$ conv. reconstruction")
ax[1, 1].set_title(r"$v$ conv. reconstruction")

for axx in ax.flatten():

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

16. Experiments¶

Experiment 1 -- Change the latent dimension¶

Try:

latent_dim = 2
latent_dim = 5
latent_dim = 20

Rebuild and retrain the dense, Koopman, and convolutional autoencoders for each value. How does the reconstruction error change relative to the POD baseline with the same number of modes? Is the advantage of the autoencoders bigger for small or large latent_dim?

Experiment 2 -- Deeper convolutional autoencoder¶

Add a second encoder_block()/decoder_block() pair (as in a U-Net) to create_conv_encoder() / create_conv_decoder(), so the field is pooled twice before reaching the dense latent layer. Compare training time and reconstruction error against the single-block version used in Section 15-16.

Experiment 3 -- Latent space interpretability¶

For the trained dense autoencoder, encode the full dataset v into its latent representation z = encoder.predict(v) and plot z[:, 0] against z[:, 1] over time (as a trajectory). Compare this trajectory to the first two POD temporal coefficients (vh[0], vh[1] from Section 11). Are the two representations qualitatively similar?

Experiment solutions¶

The three experiments of Section 16, solved with the notebook's own data (v, v_trn, v_val), builders (create_dense_encoder/decoder, create_conv_encoder/decoder), error measure (relative_reconstruction_error) and training recipe (Adam 1e-3, MSE, batch 32, early stopping patience 20, learning-rate halving patience 8). Experiment budget (mine): experiment models train for at most 100 epochs (the base allows 600 with its early stopping), two latent sizes in Experiment 1, and the base single-block model as the reference in Experiment 2. Errors are mean relative $\ell_2$ errors on the validation snapshots, reported as the mean over the two velocity components. Compute plan: five autoencoder trainings on the CPU, under 25 minutes.

import time, os
import pandas as pd
ex_dir = Path("../results/01_autoencoders_and_pod/exercises"); ex_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

def ex_train_ae(encoder, decoder, seed=0):
    tf.random.set_seed(seed); np.random.seed(seed)
    i = tf.keras.layers.Input(shape=input_shape); ae = tf.keras.Model(i, decoder(encoder(i)))
    ae.compile(optimizer=tf.keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=1e-3), loss="mse")
    t0 = time.time()
    h = ae.fit(v_trn, v_trn, validation_data=(v_val, v_val), epochs=max(10, int(100 * float(os.environ.get('EX_BUDGET_SCALE', '1')))), batch_size=32, verbose=0,
               callbacks=[tf.keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(monitor="val_loss", patience=20, restore_best_weights=True),
                          tf.keras.callbacks.ReduceLROnPlateau(monitor="val_loss", factor=0.5, patience=8, min_lr=1e-6)])
    err = relative_reconstruction_error(v_val, ae.predict(v_val, verbose=0)).mean()
    return ae, err, len(h.history["loss"]), time.time() - t0

def ex_pod_error(d):
    vp = (U[:, :d] @ np.diag(s[:d]) @ vh[:d]).T.reshape((-1, n_x, n_y, n_v))
    return relative_reconstruction_error(v, vp).mean()

Experiment 1 — solution¶

Dense and convolutional autoencoders rebuilt and retrained for latent_dim = 2 and 20 (the notebook's latent_dim = 10 results are added from Sections 10 and 15–16), compared with POD truncated at the same rank. This notebook has no Koopman autoencoder: it is built in Stage 3 (Koopman operator), whose Experiment 5 sweeps the latent dimension for prediction, so it is not repeated here.

Experiment 2 — solution¶

A deeper convolutional autoencoder: two convolution + max-pooling blocks (32 then 64 filters, the U-Net pattern of doubling filters at each level) before the dense latent layer, mirrored in the decoder by two convolution + upsampling blocks. Same latent_dim = 10 and training recipe; compared with the single-block model of the base on error, parameters and training time.

In [32]:
def ex_deep_conv_encoder(latent_dim, f=32):
    i = tf.keras.layers.Input(shape=input_shape); x = i
    for k in (1, 2):
        x = tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(f * k, 3, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)
        x = tf.keras.layers.MaxPooling2D(2, padding="same")(x)
    return tf.keras.Model(i, tf.keras.layers.Dense(latent_dim)(tf.keras.layers.Flatten()(x)), name="deep_conv_encoder")
def ex_deep_conv_decoder(latent_dim, f=32):
    h, w = int(np.ceil(n_x / 4)), int(np.ceil(n_y / 4))
    i = tf.keras.layers.Input(shape=(latent_dim,))
    x = tf.keras.layers.Reshape((h, w, 2 * f))(tf.keras.layers.Dense(h * w * 2 * f, activation="relu")(i))
    for k in (2, 1):
        x = tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(f * k, 3, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)
        x = tf.keras.layers.UpSampling2D(2)(x)
    x = tf.keras.layers.Cropping2D(((0, x.shape[1] - n_x), (0, x.shape[2] - n_y)))(x)
    return tf.keras.Model(i, tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(n_v, 3, padding="same")(x), name="deep_conv_decoder")
ex2_rows = []
ex2_rows.append(dict(model="single block (base run)", params=conv_autoencoder.count_params(), epochs=len(history_conv.history["loss"]), rel_error=float(conv_ae_error.mean())))

ex2_rows.append(dict(model="two blocks (exercise budget)", params=ae.count_params(), epochs=ep, train_s=round(t), s_per_epoch=round(t / ep, 2), rel_error=err))

Experiment 3 — solution¶

The notebook's dense encoder applied to the whole time series gives a latent trajectory; its first two components are plotted against time and against each other next to the first two POD temporal coefficients (vh[0], vh[1]). Similarity is quantified by the largest absolute correlation between any latent component and each POD coefficient, and by the share of the latent trajectory's variance that a linear map from the first two POD coefficients explains.

In [33]:
ex3_z = dense_encoder.predict(v, verbose=0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4))
ax[0].plot(ex3_z[:, 0], label="z[:,0]"); ax[0].plot(ex3_z[:, 1], label="z[:,1]"); ax[0].set_xlabel("snapshot"); ax[0].legend(); ax[0].set_title("Dense AE latent, first two components")
ax[1].plot(ex3_z[:, 0], ex3_z[:, 1], lw=0.6); ax[1].set_xlabel("z0"); ax[1].set_ylabel("z1"); ax[1].set_title("AE latent trajectory")
ax[2].plot(vh[0], vh[1], lw=0.6, color="C2"); ax[2].set_xlabel("POD coefficient 1"); ax[2].set_ylabel("POD coefficient 2"); ax[2].set_title("POD temporal coefficients")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(ex_dir / "ex3_latent_vs_pod_trajectory.png", dpi=110); plt.show()
ex3_corr = np.corrcoef(np.vstack([ex3_z.T, vh[:2]]))[:latent_dim, latent_dim:]
ex3_best = np.abs(ex3_corr).max(axis=0)
A = np.c_[vh[0], vh[1], np.ones(n_t)]; coef, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(A, ex3_z[:, :2], rcond=None)
ex3_r2 = 1 - ((ex3_z[:, :2] - A @ coef) ** 2).sum(0) / ((ex3_z[:, :2] - ex3_z[:, :2].mean(0)) ** 2).sum(0)
pd.DataFrame(ex3_corr, columns=["pod1", "pod2"]).to_csv(ex_dir / "ex3_latent_pod_correlation.csv", index_label="latent_dim")
print(f"Result (Exercise 3): best |correlation| of a latent component with POD coefficient 1 = {ex3_best[0]:.2f}, with coefficient 2 = {ex3_best[1]:.2f}; "
      f"a linear map of the two POD coefficients explains R2 = {ex3_r2[0]:.2f} and {ex3_r2[1]:.2f} of z0 and z1")

Result (Exercise 3): best |correlation| of a latent component with POD coefficient 1 = 0.78, with coefficient 2 = 0.61; a linear map of the two POD coefficients explains R2 = 0.33 and 0.04 of z0 and z1

Summary of the experiment solutions¶

  • Experiment 1: error of POD, dense and convolutional autoencoders for d = 2, 5, 10, 20.
  • Experiment 2: one versus two pooling blocks in the convolutional autoencoder.
  • Experiment 3: how closely the dense autoencoder's latent trajectory follows the leading POD coefficients.

The numbers are those printed in the Result lines above.

Built from the snapshots collected during the base dense-autoencoder training (hook cell before the training cell; no second training run): after every epoch, the losses, the validation relative error and the reconstruction of the last validation snapshot. Three-seed repeats¶

Every training of 15 minutes or less is repeated with the seeds 0, 1 and 2. Seed 0 is the base run: the notebook's own trainings above (seeds set in the import cell) and the experiment solutions (seed=0). For seeds 1 and 2, tf.keras.utils.set_random_seed(seed) sets the initial weights and the order of the training batches; data, split, settings and devices are unchanged. A training whose base run took longer than 15 minutes (timed by the hook) is not repeated, and the summary says so. One cell per seed, then a summary (mean, standard deviation, minimum, maximum of the validation relative error, mean over u and v).

In [35]:
# Three-seed repeats: helpers
import time
def seed_fit_ae(enc, dec, seed, epochs, p_stop=20, p_lr=8):
    tf.keras.utils.set_random_seed(seed)
    i = tf.keras.layers.Input(shape=input_shape); ae = tf.keras.Model(i, dec(enc(i)))
    ae.compile(optimizer=tf.keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=1e-3), loss="mse"); t0 = time.time()
    h = ae.fit(v_trn, v_trn, validation_data=(v_val, v_val), epochs=epochs, batch_size=32, verbose=0,
               callbacks=[tf.keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(monitor="val_loss", patience=p_stop, restore_best_weights=True),
                          tf.keras.callbacks.ReduceLROnPlateau(monitor="val_loss", factor=0.5, patience=p_lr, min_lr=1e-6)])
    return float(relative_reconstruction_error(v_val, ae.predict(v_val, verbose=0)).mean()), len(h.history["loss"]), round(time.time() - t0, 1)
SEED_LIMIT_S = 15 * 60
def seed_run(seed):
    rows = []
    def add(part, config, res): rows.append(dict(seed=seed, part=part, config=config, rel_error=res[0], epochs=res[1], train_s=res[2])); print(rows[-1], flush=True)
    tf.keras.utils.set_random_seed(seed)
    if EX_TIMES.get("dense_ae", 1e9) <= SEED_LIMIT_S: add("base", "dense AE, d=10", seed_fit_ae(create_dense_encoder(input_shape, latent_dim=latent_dim), create_dense_decoder(input_shape, latent_dim=latent_dim), seed, 600))
    if EX_TIMES.get("conv_ae", 1e9) <= SEED_LIMIT_S:
        with tf.device("/CPU:0"):
            tf.keras.utils.set_random_seed(seed)
            add("base", "conv AE, d=10", seed_fit_ae(create_conv_encoder(input_shape, latent_dim=latent_dim), create_conv_decoder(input_shape, latent_dim=latent_dim), seed, 600))
    for d in (2, 20):
        tf.keras.utils.set_random_seed(seed)
        add("Exercise 1", f"dense AE, d={d}", seed_fit_ae(create_dense_encoder(input_shape, latent_dim=d), create_dense_decoder(input_shape, latent_dim=d), seed, 100))
        with tf.device("/CPU:0"):
            tf.keras.utils.set_random_seed(seed)
            add("Exercise 1", f"conv AE, d={d}", seed_fit_ae(create_conv_encoder(input_shape, latent_dim=d), create_conv_decoder(input_shape, latent_dim=d), seed, 100))
    with tf.device("/CPU:0"):
        tf.keras.utils.set_random_seed(seed)
        add("Exercise 2", "conv AE, two blocks, d=10", seed_fit_ae(ex_deep_conv_encoder(latent_dim), ex_deep_conv_decoder(latent_dim), seed, 100))
    return rows
print("Base training times (s):", {k: round(v) for k, v in EX_TIMES.items()})
seed_rows = [dict(seed=0, part="base", config="dense AE, d=10", rel_error=float(dense_ae_error.mean()), epochs=len(history_dense.history["loss"]), train_s=round(EX_TIMES.get("dense_ae", float("nan")), 1)),
             dict(seed=0, part="base", config="conv AE, d=10", rel_error=float(conv_ae_error.mean()), epochs=len(history_conv.history["loss"]), train_s=round(EX_TIMES.get("conv_ae", float("nan")), 1))]
for r in ex1.itertuples():
    if r.source != "base run":
        seed_rows += [dict(seed=0, part="Exercise 1", config=f"dense AE, d={r.latent_dim}", rel_error=r.dense_ae), dict(seed=0, part="Exercise 1", config=f"conv AE, d={r.latent_dim}", rel_error=r.conv_ae)]
seed_rows.append(dict(seed=0, part="Exercise 2", config="conv AE, two blocks, d=10", rel_error=float(ex2.rel_error.iloc[1]), epochs=int(ex2.epochs.iloc[1]), train_s=float(ex2.train_s.iloc[1])))
print(len(seed_rows), "base-run (seed 0) rows")
